HiSTOR: Structured Treatment-outcome Representation Learning for High-Dimensional Longitudinal Data

Chuanqi Lao Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The University of Texas at Arlington    Junzhou Huang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The University of Texas at Arlington    Qiao Liu Affiliation: Department of Biostatistics, Yale School of Public Health, Yale University*Corresponding author: qiao.liu@yale.edu
Abstract

Estimating potential outcomes under alternative treatment sequences is essential for personalized decision-making, but remains challenging with high-dimensional covariates and time-varying confounding. In this study, we propose HiSTOR (High-dimensional Structured Treatment-Outcome Representation), an end-to-end framework that integrates nonlinear dimension reduction with longitudinal counterfactual prediction. The central idea is to learn structured low-dimensional representations of both current patient states and evolving histories, according to their shared and distinct relationships with treatment assignment and outcomes. This extends latent-space covariate adjustment to longitudinal settings, jointly addressing covariate dimensionality and historical complexity. The resulting framework supports one-step and multi-step outcome prediction under specified treatment sequences. Experiments on CVSim and CancerSim demonstrate the superiority of HiSTOR across varying covariate dimensions, confounding strengths, and prediction horizons compared to state-of-the-art methods. To sum up, HiSTOR offers a unified approach to connecting high-dimensional covariate adjustment with longitudinal potential-outcome prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/liuq-lab/HiSTOR.

1 Introduction

Personalized treatment planning requires predicting outcomes under alternative treatment sequences from longitudinal observations. This problem is fundamentally challenging because treatment decisions may depend on time-varying covariates that also affect future outcomes and may themselves be influenced by prior treatments. The difficulty is further amplified in modern biomedical applications, where each patient is characterized by high-dimensional and strongly correlated measurements accumulated over time (Allam et al., 2021; Bica et al., 2021; Battalio et al., 2021; Murray et al., 2016). As the covariate dimension and observation history grow, effective counterfactual prediction therefore requires methods that can effectively compress patient information while retaining what is relevant to both treatment assignment and outcome prediction.

Recent modern AI approaches to longitudinal counterfactual prediction address time-varying confounding through reweighting, representation balancing, sequential outcome modeling, or recursive regression (Lim, 2018; Bica et al., 2020; Melnychuk et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021; Xiong et al., 2024; Hess et al., 2026). These methods primarily focus on how longitudinal histories should be adjusted, balanced, or propagated over time. Less attention has been paid to how high-dimensional covariates and accumulated histories should be jointly compressed and represented for treatment-conditioned outcome prediction.

To address the high-dimensional covariate and confounding challenges, we propose HiSTOR (High-dimensional Structured Treatment-Outcome Representation), an end-to-end framework for structured representation learning in high-dimensional longitudinal settings (Figure 1). The key idea of HiSTOR is to separately represent the current high-dimensional patient state and the preceding longitudinal history, and then organize their fusion into a task-structured low-dimensional latent space. This representation preserves information relevant to treatment assignment and outcome prediction. By explicitly separating current-state compression from historical representation learning, HiSTOR provides a unified representation for longitudinal covariate adjustment and treatment-conditioned outcome prediction. We summarize our main contributions as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a structured representation-learning framework for high-dimensional longitudinal causal inference that encodes the current patient state and preceding history by their roles in the treatment and outcome mechanisms.

  • •

    We extend structured latent covariate adjustment from cross-sectional to longitudinal settings and develop flexible prediction mechanisms for both one-step and multi-step treatment-conditioned potential outcomes.

  • •

    We demonstrate strong empirical performance of HiSTOR across varying confounding strengths, covariate dimensions, and prediction horizons. HiSTOR achieves the lowest mean one-step and five-horizon-average errors across all tested CancerSim confounding strengths, and the lowest five-horizon-average errors across all tested CVSim covariate dimensions.

2 Related Work

Traditional longitudinal causal inference. Static estimators learn potential outcomes from covariate-treatment-outcome observations (Johansson et al., 2016; Alaa and Schaar, 2018; Wager and Athey, 2018; Yoon et al., 2018; Curth and Van der Schaar, 2021), whereas longitudinal methods condition on evolving patient histories. Classical approaches include marginal structural models and G-computation (Robins, 1986; Robins et al., 2000; Robins and Hernan, 2008). These approaches provide the statistical foundation for longitudinal causal inference, but their direct application can become challenging with complex, high-dimensional patient histories.

Modern AI for longitudinal counterfactual prediction. Recent work integrates these causal principles with flexible neural models for learning treatment effects from longitudinal data. RMSN combines recurrent outcome models with stabilized inverse-probability weights (Lim, 2018). CRN uses treatment-adversarial training to balance recurrent histories, and CT uses a multi-input Transformer with domain confusion (Bica et al., 2020; Melnychuk et al., 2022). Causal CPC combines recurrent encoding, contrastive predictive coding, and representation balancing (Bouchattaoui et al., 2024); CTD-NKO uses treatment-dependent neural Koopman dynamics and distributional weighting (Wang et al., 2025). G-Net and G-Transformer estimate future-variable distributions for G-computation (Li et al., 2021; Xiong et al., 2024), while IGC-Net recursively regresses pseudo-outcomes without modeling complete future-covariate distributions (Hess et al., 2026). These approaches advance complementary aspects of confounding adjustment, temporal representation learning, and treatment-conditioned forecasting.

Structured representation learning for causal inference.

In cross-sectional settings, DR-CFR learns treatment-related, outcome-related, and shared representations (Hassanpour and Greiner, 2019), while TEDVAE separates instrumental, confounding, and outcome risk factors (Zhang et al., 2021). CausalEGM, CausalBGM, and BGM-IV combine structured latent modeling with high-dimensional covariate adjustment through encoding-generative or Bayesian formulations (Liu et al., 2024; Liu and Wong, 2026b; Luo and Liu, 2026). These methods do not model repeated treatments or evolving patient histories.

Positioning of HiSTOR.

HiSTOR addresses this longitudinal prediction task with a focus on high-dimensional patient covariates. Its contribution is to couple explicit covariate compression with a latent-space partition designed for both prediction and reconstruction. The partition combines shared and task-specific predictive components with a dedicated residual reconstruction component, linking the organization of treatment-outcome information with information retention under compression. This design brings together structured covariate adjustment and longitudinal representation learning for patient histories containing many correlated covariates.

3 Problem Formulation

Let 𝒟={{Vi​t,Xi​t,Yi​t}t=1Ti}i=1N\mathcal{D}=\{\{V_{it},X_{it},Y_{it}\}_{t=1}^{T_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{N} contain independent patient trajectories. Here Vi​tV_{it} denotes the covariates available before treatment at time tt, including baseline components and, when present, time-varying components; Xi​tX_{it} is the observed treatment; and Yi​tY_{it} is the associated post-treatment outcome. Suppressing ii, the observed history before treatment at time tt is

ℋt=(X<t,Y<t,V≤t).\mathcal{H}_{t}=(X_{<t},Y_{<t},V_{\leq t}). (1)

Here ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} is the observed history, whereas ht−1h_{t-1} is the representation of the preceding trajectory through time t−1t-1. Appendix A summarizes the notation and temporal alignment.

Following the longitudinal potential-outcomes framework (Robins, 1986; Robins and Hernan, 2008), let Yt​(x)Y_{t}(x) be the outcome under treatment xx at time tt with prior treatments observed. For history hh and a specified sequence x¯=xt:t+τ−1\bar{x}=x_{t:t+\tau-1}, the targets are

{μt​(x,h)=𝔼⁡[Yt​(x)∣ℋt=h],μt(τ)​(x¯,h)=𝔼⁡[Yt+τ−1​(x¯)∣ℋt=h].\left\{\begin{aligned} \mu_{t}(x,h)&=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{t}(x)\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}=h\right],\\ \mu_{t}^{(\tau)}(\bar{x},h)&=\mathbb{E}\!\left[Y_{t+\tau-1}(\bar{x})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}=h\right].\end{aligned}\right. (2)

Thus τ=1\tau=1 reduces to the one-step target. At prediction time only ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} and the specified treatment sequence are available, while future outcomes and covariates are not.

Identification from observational data requires longitudinal consistency, positivity, and sequential ignorability (Robins et al., 2000; Robins and Hernan, 2008). For t≤s≤ut\leq s\leq u and an intervention sequence xs:ux_{s:u}, we state these conditions as

{Yu(Xs:u)=Yu(Consistency),Pr⁡(Xs=xs∣ℋs=hs)>0(Positivity),Xs⟂⟂Yu(xs:u)∣ℋs(Sequential ignorability).\left\{\begin{aligned} &Y_{u}(X_{s:u})=Y_{u}&&\text{(Consistency)},\\ &\Pr(X_{s}=x_{s}\mid\mathcal{H}_{s}=h_{s})>0&&\text{(Positivity)},\\ &X_{s}\perp\!\!\!\perp Y_{u}(x_{s:u})\mid\mathcal{H}_{s}&&\text{(Sequential ignorability)}.\end{aligned}\right. (3)

Positivity is required for intervention-relevant treatments at histories that can arise under the intervention, while sequential ignorability assumes no unmeasured treatment-outcome confounding conditional on ℋs\mathcal{H}_{s}. Under these assumptions, the targets in Equation 2 are identified within the standard longitudinal potential-outcome framework.

4 Methods

4.1 Covariate and History Encoding

At each decision time tt, HiSTOR encodes the pre-treatment information in ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} through two complementary paths: a covariate encoder for the current covariates VtV_{t}, and a causally masked temporal network for the preceding trajectory.

The covariate encoder eVe_{V} maps the current covariates to a low-dimensional representation ct=eV​(Vt)c_{t}=e_{V}(V_{t}). The temporal network 𝒯\mathcal{T} summarizes the trajectory preceding treatment XtX_{t}. At sequence position tt, it receives the treatment, outcome, and covariate encoding from the previous time step, which are embedded and summed into an input token. 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a stack of BB Transformer decoder blocks and produces the embedding ht−1=𝒯⁡(X<t,Y<t,V<t)h_{t-1}=\mathcal{T}(X_{<t},Y_{<t},V_{<t}). The attention masks ensure that ht−1h_{t-1} uses only information available through time t−1t-1. The current covariate encoding ctc_{t} and preceding trajectory representation ht−1h_{t-1} are subsequently fused and mapped into the structured latent space.

4.2 Structured Latent Representation

Treatment assignment and outcomes may depend on overlapping but distinct aspects of the pre-treatment history. A single entangled representation does not distinguish such structure. To consider this, HiSTOR fuses the current covariate encoding and preceding trajectory representation, then maps their concatenation into a partitioned latent space:

Φt=[ht−1,ct],Zt=Q⁡(Φt)=[zt0,zt1,zt2,zt3].\Phi_{t}=[h_{t-1},c_{t}],\qquad Z_{t}=Q(\Phi_{t})=[z_{t}^{0},z_{t}^{1},z_{t}^{2},z_{t}^{3}]. (4)

zt0z_{t}^{0} is provided to both the treatment and outcome prediction heads. This encourages zt0z_{t}^{0} to retain information in the observed history that is predictive of both treatment assignment and outcomes, and is therefore most directly relevant to confounding adjustment. In contrast, zt1z_{t}^{1} is used only for outcome prediction and zt2z_{t}^{2} only for treatment prediction, allowing outcome-specific and treatment-specific variation to be learned. The remaining latent component zt3z_{t}^{3} is trained through residual reconstruction, providing additional capacity to preserve irrelevant covariate information.

4.3 Learning the Structured Representation

The partition in equation 4 does not by itself determine the functional role of each latent component. HiSTOR induces this structure through task-specific supervision that controls which components are available to the treatment and outcome prediction heads.

For a specified treatment xtx_{t}, the outcome and auxiliary treatment predictions are

y^t​(xt)=fY​([zt0,zt1,xt]),𝝅^t=fX​([zt0,zt2]),\widehat{y}_{t}(x_{t})=f_{Y}([z_{t}^{0},z_{t}^{1},x_{t}]),\qquad\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}_{t}=f_{X}([z_{t}^{0},z_{t}^{2}]), (5)

where 𝝅^t\widehat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}_{t} denotes the predicted treatment-assignment distribution. The treatment head is used only to supervise representation learning. The outcome head always conditions on the observed or externally specified treatment xtx_{t}, rather than on the auxiliary treatment prediction.

During training, the outcome head is optimized using the factual outcome loss ℒY\mathcal{L}_{Y}, while the treatment head is optimized using the auxiliary treatment loss ℒX\mathcal{L}_{X}. The residual component zt3z_{t}^{3} is trained through reconstruction. Together, these objectives learn the structured representation end-to-end, while the complete loss definitions and regularization terms are given in Section 4.4.

4.4 Training Objectives

HiSTOR jointly trains the current-state encoder, temporal network, structured mapping, prediction heads, and reconstruction modules. The overall objective combines factual outcome prediction, auxiliary treatment prediction, reconstruction, and representation regularization:

ℒtotal=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}={} ℒY+λX​ℒX+λr​e​c​ℒrec+λadv​(e)​ℒadv+λnorm​ℒnorm+λroll​ℒroll.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{Y}+\lambda_{X}\mathcal{L}_{X}+\lambda_{rec}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}(e)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{norm}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{norm}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{roll}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}}. (6)

Here, ℒY\mathcal{L}_{Y} and ℒX\mathcal{L}_{X} are introduced in Equation 5. The reconstruction objective ℒrec\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}} encourages the compressed representation to retain information about the observed patient state and provides supervision for the residual component zt3z_{t}^{3}. The distribution-matching loss ℒadv\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}} regularizes the learned current-state representation, while ℒnorm\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{norm}} controls its scale. This combination of reconstruction and distribution matching is also used in bidirectional generative modeling (Liu et al., 2021).

To reduce train-prediction discrepancy, we optionally introduce a rollout loss ℒroll\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}} that recursively applies the one-step predictor over factual multi-step windows and propagates its predictions through subsequent histories. Complete definitions of the reconstruction, distribution-matching, rollout, and weighting objectives are provided in Appendix B.

4.5 One-Step and Multi-Step Prediction

For a specified treatment xtx_{t}, the one-step prediction is

μ^θ(1)​(xt,ℋt)=fY​([zt0,zt1,xt]),\widehat{\mu}_{\theta}^{(1)}(x_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t})=f_{Y}([z_{t}^{0},z_{t}^{1},x_{t}]), (7)

where θ\theta denotes the fitted model parameters and ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} is the observed pre-treatment history. This is the prediction y^t​(xt)\widehat{y}_{t}(x_{t}) defined in Equation 5. Alternative treatments change xtx_{t} while retaining the same pre-treatment information.

Autoregressive prediction.

For a treatment plan x¯=xt:t+τ−1\bar{x}=x_{t:t+\tau-1} of length τ\tau, we recursively predict

y^sAR=μ^θ(1)(xs,ℋ^s),s=t,…,t+τ−1,\widehat{y}_{s}^{\mathrm{AR}}=\widehat{\mu}_{\theta}^{(1)}(x_{s},\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{s}),\qquad s=t,\ldots,t+\tau-1, (8)

where ℋ^s\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{s} combines the observed history up to the prediction origin, the specified treatment sequence, and previously generated outcomes. For V~t\widetilde{V}_{t}, static covariates are reused unchanged while time-varying covariate inputs are carried forward from their last observed values at the prediction origin. This autoregressive construction can accommodate arbitrary prediction horizons, but its recursive dependence on model-generated outcomes allows prediction errors to propagate across future steps.

Parallel decoding.

To avoid recursive outcome feedback, HiSTOR also supports direct multi-step prediction. Given the structured representation ZtZ_{t} at the prediction origin and a specified treatment plan x¯=xt:t+τ−1\bar{x}=x_{t:t+\tau-1}, a decoder predicts the complete outcome trajectory in a single forward pass:

(y^tD,…,y^t+τ−1D)=Dτ​(Zt,x¯).(\widehat{y}_{t}^{\mathrm{D}},\ldots,\widehat{y}_{t+\tau-1}^{\mathrm{D}})=D_{\tau}(Z_{t},\bar{x}). (9)

The decoder uses a shared representation of the treatment plan together with horizon-specific outcome heads. It is trained additionally on factual multi-step windows. Thus, autoregressive and parallel decoding provide complementary strategies for extending the same structured representation to longitudinal treatment-conditioned prediction.

Appendix D specifies the dataset-specific preparation at the forecast origin, and Appendix B gives the direct-decoder architecture.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

We evaluate HiSTOR on two simulated longitudinal benchmarks with known counterfactual outcomes. CancerSim models tumor volume under four treatment options: no treatment, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and their combination, with treatment-assignment confounding strength γ∈{0,1,2,3,4}\gamma\in\{0,1,2,3,4\} (Geng et al., 2017; Bica et al., 2020; Melnychuk et al., 2022; Hess et al., 2026). We use 10,000 training patients, 1,000 validation patients, and two separately generated 1,000-patient cohorts for one-step and multi-step testing. CVSim augments seven base covariates with dhd∈{0,10,20,50,100,200,500,1000,2000}d_{\mathrm{hd}}\in\{0,10,20,50,100,200,500,1000,2000\} correlated noisy covariates while keeping the underlying trajectory-generating process fixed. The additional covariates remain fixed within patients in the Static setting and vary over time in the Temporal setting. We split 5,000 patient trajectories into training, validation, and test sets using an 80/10/10 patient-level split. Appendix C provides the data-generation details. To complement these controlled simulation studies, we also include a semi-synthetic evaluation based on de-identified MIMIC-III covariates; its data construction, evaluation protocol, and results are reported in Appendix I.

Prediction tasks.

We evaluate independent one-step prediction at observed histories and multi-step prediction under fixed treatment plans, without access to future observed outcomes or covariates. The multi-step plans prescribe sustained combined therapy in CancerSim and treatment category 2 in CVSim. Both benchmarks evaluate five future positions: CVSim scores horizons τ=1\tau=1 to 55, whereas CancerSim scores τ=2\tau=2 to 66 after an unscored boundary prediction under the factual treatment. For HiSTOR, the one-step benchmark uses the outcome head, and the main multi-step comparisons use the direct decoder. Autoregressive prediction is evaluated in the ablation study. Appendix D specifies the treatment plans, forecast boundaries, and input preparation.

Baselines.

We compare HiSTOR with MSM (Robins et al., 2000), RMSN (Lim, 2018), CRN (Bica et al., 2020), CT (Melnychuk et al., 2022), Causal CPC (Bouchattaoui et al., 2024), CTD-NKO (Wang et al., 2025), and IGC-Net (Hess et al., 2026). Within each experimental condition, all methods use the same data realization, patient splits, and evaluation protocol. Baseline configurations are provided in Appendix F.

Evaluation and reporting.

For the primary CancerSim and CVSim experiments, we report normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE), using the tumor-death volume threshold for CancerSim and the task-specific test-target range for CVSim. These results are summarized as the mean and sample standard deviation across five random seeds, {3,101,42,8,9}\{3,101,42,8,9\}. For multi-step evaluation, we average the five horizon-specific NRMSE values within each seed before aggregating across seeds. Independent one-step evaluation and the first multi-step horizon use distinct evaluation protocols. HiSTOR’s backbone and direct-decoder checkpoints are selected using their respective factual validation objectives, with counterfactual test targets excluded from model selection. Appendices E and B provide the metric definitions and optimization details, respectively.

5.2 Outcome Prediction under Varying Confounding

We evaluate HiSTOR on CancerSim across confounding strengths γ=0\gamma=0 to 44 for independent one-step prediction and multi-step prediction under sustained combined therapy. For each condition, relative improvements are calculated against the baseline with the lowest mean NRMSE.

HiSTOR achieves the lowest mean one-step NRMSE at all five confounding strengths, with relative reductions ranging from 4.2%4.2\% to 13.4%13.4\% (Table 1). The gains are more significant under stronger confounding. At γ=3\gamma=3, HiSTOR reduces NRMSE from 0.71220.7122 for CTD-NKO to 0.61650.6165, corresponding to a 13.4%13.4\% reduction. At γ=4\gamma=4, it reduces NRMSE from 0.76200.7620 to 0.67030.6703 relative to the same strongest baseline, yielding a 12.0%12.0\% reduction. These gains exceed the 4.2%4.2\%–5.2%5.2\% reductions observed at γ=0\gamma=0 and 11, indicating a larger predictive advantage when treatment assignment is more strongly confounded.

For multi-step prediction, HiSTOR achieves the lowest five-horizon-average NRMSE at every confounding strength (Table 2). Its relative improvement over the strongest baseline increases steadily from 6.5%6.5\% at γ=0\gamma=0 to 14.9%14.9\% at γ=4\gamma=4. In the strongest-confounding setting, HiSTOR reduces the five-horizon average from 1.07011.0701 for the strongest baseline Causal CPC to 0.91050.9105. This advantage of HiSTOR is also consistent across multiple repeated runs with different random seeds at each confounding strength for the five-horizon average (Appendix G.1).

The horizon-specific results further demonstrate that the improvement extends across the prediction window. As shown in Figure 2, HiSTOR achieves the lowest mean NRMSE across all 25 combinations of confounding strength and prediction horizon. For example, at γ=4\gamma=4 and τ=4\tau=4, HiSTOR reduces NRMSE from 1.05911.0591 for Causal CPC to 0.87720.8772, a relative reduction of 17.2%17.2\%. Although the strongest competing method varies across horizons, HiSTOR consistently achieves the lowest mean NRMSE, complementing the aggregate multi-step results. Complete horizon-specific results and paired seed-level comparisons are provided in Appendix G.

5.3 Outcome Prediction with High-Dimensional Covariates

We evaluate HiSTOR on CVSim as the number of correlated noisy covariates increases, while holding the underlying trajectory-generating process fixed. In the Static setting, the additional covariates remain fixed within each patient, assessing prediction in the presence of redundant high-dimensional measurements. In the Temporal setting, these covariates additionally exhibit temporal drift and time-specific noise, assessing prediction when the added measurements also vary over time. Both settings evaluate independent one-step prediction and multi-step prediction under sustained treatment.

For CVSim one-step prediction, HiSTOR achieves the lowest mean NRMSE at all evaluated dimensions from dhd=200d_{\mathrm{hd}}=200 to 20002000 in both settings (Figure 3(a,c)). At dhd=2000d_{\mathrm{hd}}=2000, HiSTOR reduces NRMSE from 0.9540.954 for the best baseline IGC-Net to 0.8820.882 in the Static setting and from 0.9410.941 to 0.8450.845 in the Temporal setting, corresponding to relative reductions of 7.5%7.5\% and 10.2%10.2\%. Although IGC-Net has the lowest mean error at dhd=10d_{\mathrm{hd}}=10-100100, HiSTOR leads at dhd=0d_{\mathrm{hd}}=0 and across all the higher-dimensional settings. Its one-step advantage is therefore most consistent when the observed covariate space is large. These results highlight HiSTOR’s predictive advantage in settings with high-dimensional, correlated covariates.

HiSTOR shows a more consistent advantage for multi-step prediction, achieving the lowest five-horizon-average NRMSE in all 18 combinations of covariate dimension and Static/Temporal setting (Figure 3(b,d)). At dhd=2000d_{\mathrm{hd}}=2000, HiSTOR reduces NRMSE by 28.4%28.4\% in Static and 14.3%14.3\% in Temporal relative to baseline Causal CPC, the strongest baseline under this metric in both settings. The advantage also extends across individual prediction horizons: HiSTOR achieves the lowest mean NRMSE in 71 of the 72 conditions with τ≥2\tau\geq 2. The only exception is Static dhd=20d_{\mathrm{hd}}=20 at τ=2\tau=2, where CTD-NKO has a slightly lower mean error.

At the highest evaluated dimension, dhd=2000d_{\mathrm{hd}}=2000, HiSTOR achieves the lowest mean error for both one-step prediction and all five multi-step horizons in both settings (Table 3). At τ=2\tau=2, its NRMSE reductions relative to the strongest baseline reach 32.5%32.5\% in Static and 16.9%16.9\% in Temporal. These gains persist through the final evaluated horizon, with corresponding reductions of 22.0%22.0\% and 8.7%8.7\% at τ=5\tau=5. Together, these results highlight HiSTOR’s advantage in forecasting treatment-conditioned trajectories with high-dimensional covariates, whether the additional measurements remain fixed or vary over time. Complete results are provided in Appendix H.

5.4 Ablation Study

We assess the contributions of HiSTOR’s components using the CancerSim benchmark at confounding strengths γ=1\gamma=1 and 44. We separately remove the covariate encoding bottleneck, distribution-matching regularization, and reconstruction objectives. We also replace direct multi-step decoding with autoregressive prediction. Table 4 summarizes the results over five seeds. All relative error increases below are calculated against the full model at the corresponding confounding strength. The full model achieves the lowest mean error in every reported comparison. Removing the covariate bottleneck produces the largest increases in multi-step errors. The five-horizon-average NRMSE rises from 0.52910.5291 to 0.56640.5664 at γ=1\gamma=1 and from 0.91050.9105 to 0.95550.9555 at γ=4\gamma=4, corresponding to relative increases of 7.0%7.0\% and 4.9%4.9\%. The corresponding one-step errors increase by 4.7%4.7\% and 1.4%1.4\%. These results identify the covariate bottleneck as the most influential component among those evaluated, with benefits across both prediction tasks and confounding strengths.

Distribution matching and reconstruction provide additional improvements whose magnitudes depend on the setting. Removing distribution matching increases the five-horizon-average NRMSE by 4.3%4.3\% at γ=1\gamma=1 and 0.9%0.9\% at γ=4\gamma=4. Removing the reconstruction objectives increases the same metric by 3.8%3.8\% and 0.5%0.5\%, respectively. Both modifications also increase the mean one-step error. Thus, these objectives contribute to predictive performance, although their effects are smaller than those of the covariate bottleneck in the evaluated settings.

Finally, replacing parallel decoding with autoregressive prediction increases the five-horizon-average NRMSE by 4.0%4.0\% at γ=1\gamma=1 and 1.0%1.0\% at γ=4\gamma=4. This result indicates the benefit of direct multi-step parallel decoding compared to autoregressive predictions where the error may accumulate across multi-steps.

6 Conclusion

We introduced HiSTOR, a structured representation learning framework for longitudinal counterfactual outcome prediction with high-dimensional covariates. HiSTOR combines current-covariate compression with masked history encoding and partitions their fusion into shared, outcome-specific, treatment-specific, and residual components. Joint predictive and reconstruction objectives encourage distinct functional roles and retention of information about the observed patient state. Across CancerSim and CVSim, HiSTOR achieves the lowest mean five-horizon-average NRMSE in every evaluated setting, with one-step advantages across CancerSim confounding strengths and at higher CVSim dimensions.

Our evaluation currently focuses on simulated and semi-synthetic benchmarks. Future work will extend evaluation to real-world clinical data and broader treatment regimes, explore separate modeling of future covariate dynamics, and incorporate uncertainty quantification (Liu and Wong, 2026a; Liu, 2026). We will also investigate when compressed histories retain sufficient information for confounding adjustment.

Appendix A Notation and Temporal Alignment

For one patient, the information available before treatment at time tt is

ℋt=(X<t,Y<t,V≤t).\mathcal{H}_{t}=(X_{<t},Y_{<t},V_{\leq t}).

The model processes this information through two complementary paths. The temporal path constructs ht−1h_{t-1} from the shifted sequence of preceding treatments, outcomes, and current-state encodings. The current-state path separately constructs ctc_{t} from the dataset-specific raw input WtW_{t}. These representations are fused as

Φt=[ht−1,ct],Zt=Q⁡(Φt).\Phi_{t}=[h_{t-1},c_{t}],\qquad Z_{t}=Q(\Phi_{t}).

The symbol WtW_{t} is used only for implementation details in the appendix. Its construction differs across datasets and is specified in Appendix C. In all cases, it contains only information observed before treatment XtX_{t}.

At sequence position tt, the shifted inputs Xt−1X_{t-1}, Yt−1Y_{t-1}, and ct−1c_{t-1} are combined into the fused history token sts_{t}. Fixed positional encodings are added only to the token sequence. The projected sequence Wmc0:T−1W_{m}c_{0:T-1} forms the cross-attention memory and receives no positional encoding. The causal mask permits position tt to attend only to positions j≤tj\leq t, while MpadM_{\mathrm{pad}} excludes inactive padded positions. Because the inputs are shifted by one position, the resulting output ht−1h_{t-1} summarizes observations only through time t−1t-1.

The auxiliary treatment head outputs logits ℓtX\ell_{t}^{X}, which are converted into categorical probabilities by

ptX=softmax⁡(ℓtX).p_{t}^{X}=\operatorname{softmax}(\ell_{t}^{X}).

If a hard auxiliary prediction is needed, it is obtained as

x^t=arg⁡maxk⁡pt,kX.\widehat{x}_{t}=\arg\max_{k}p_{t,k}^{X}.

This auxiliary prediction does not provide the treatment input to the outcome model. One-step outcome prediction instead conditions on the observed or externally specified treatment xtx_{t}.

For one-step prediction, the model uses the information available at the prediction origin and predicts YtY_{t} under the observed or specified treatment xtx_{t}. For multi-step prediction, the model receives a specified treatment sequence and does not use future outcomes or future covariates. The first output of a multi-step evaluation may use different patient origins from the aggregate independent one-step benchmark and therefore need not reproduce the same statistic. Dataset-specific input construction is described in Appendix C, while sequence initialization and forecast-boundary preparation are described in Appendices B and D.

Appendix B Architecture and Objectives

Structured branch configuration.

We set (d0,d1,d2,d3)=(24,24,48,64)(d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3})=(24,24,48,64), giving dZ=160d_{Z}=160. The same allocation is used for all datasets. During backbone training, dropout is applied to [zt0,zt2][z_{t}^{0},z_{t}^{2}] before the auxiliary treatment head. Both simulation datasets use categorical treatment prediction. The direct multi-step decoder uses all four branches as its representation context.

Representation and temporal configuration.

Both simulation adapters use du=128d_{u}=128, dc=16d_{c}=16, dh=128d_{h}=128, and dZ=160d_{Z}=160, so that QQ maps ℝ144\mathbb{R}^{144} to ℝ160\mathbb{R}^{160}. The raw input width dWd_{W} depends on the dataset and input configuration. The treatment and outcome embedding MLPs each have two hidden layers of width 256 and output width 128. The structured mapping likewise has two hidden layers of width 256. The temporal backbone has four Transformer decoder blocks, four attention heads per block, a feedforward width of 256, and dropout 0.15. Fixed sinusoidal positional encodings are added only to the fused tokens; the projected current-state memory has no added positional encoding. Both attention paths apply the same causal and key-padding masks. The direct prediction decoder uses a boundary and GRU hidden width of 32, a treatment embedding width of 8, and a separate outcome head with hidden width 32 for each horizon.

Current-state projection and reconstruction objectives.

The main text writes the current-state encoding at a high level as ct=eV​(Vt)c_{t}=e_{V}(V_{t}). In the implementation, this encoding is computed from the dataset-specific input WtW_{t} using a projection followed by the encoder:

ut=P⁡(Wt),ct=EV​(ut).u_{t}=P(W_{t}),\qquad c_{t}=E_{V}(u_{t}).

Thus, eVe_{V} in the main text is shorthand for the implementation-level mapping. The input WtW_{t} is dataset-specific: CVSim uses Wt=VtW_{t}=V_{t}, whereas CancerSim uses Wi​t=[Yi,t−1,Si]W_{it}=[Y_{i,t-1},S_{i}], as defined in Appendix C.

They are connected by two first-level reconstruction objectives:

u^t=GV​(ct),W^tstd=Draw​(ct),ℒemb=MSE⁡(u^,u),ℒraw=MSE⁡(W^std,Wstd).\widehat{u}_{t}=G_{V}(c_{t}),\qquad\widehat{W}_{t}^{\mathrm{std}}=D_{\mathrm{raw}}(c_{t}),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{emb}}=\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat{u},u),\quad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{raw}}=\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat{W}^{\mathrm{std}},W^{\mathrm{std}}). (10)

Here GVG_{V} is the embedding decoder and DrawD_{\mathrm{raw}} reconstructs the standardized raw input. Both losses are averaged over valid patient–time pairs. The raw reconstruction targets are standardized using training-set statistics that remain fixed during validation and testing.

The residual-reconstruction target is the embedding information left unreconstructed by the first-level decoder:

rt=sg⁡[ut−GV​(ct)],ℒres=MSE⁡(R⁡(zt3),rt),r_{t}=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[u_{t}-G_{V}(c_{t})\right],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{res}}=\operatorname{MSE}\!\left(R(z_{t}^{3}),r_{t}\right), (11)

where sg\operatorname{sg} blocks gradients through the residual target. The complete reconstruction objective is

ℒrec=ℒemb+ℒraw+ℒres.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{emb}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{raw}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{res}}. (12)

The embedding decoder GVG_{V} also maps standard-normal samples into the embedding space for the adversarial distributional objective in Equation 16.

Projection branches.

Both projection branches are used in the experiments. CancerSim and the five CVSim settings with dhd≤100d_{\mathrm{hd}}\leq 100 use fixed sinusoidal features followed by an MLP. The feature expansion concatenates WtW_{t} with sin⁡(2k​Wt)\sin(2^{k}W_{t}) and cos⁡(2k​Wt)\cos(2^{k}W_{t}) for k=0,…,7k=0,\ldots,7, and each of the two hidden layers has width max⁡(⌊17​dW/2⌋,128)\max(\lfloor 17d_{W}/2\rfloor,128). The four CVSim settings with dhd≥200d_{\mathrm{hd}}\geq 200 use an MLP directly on WtW_{t}, with two hidden layers of width max⁡(dW,128)\max(d_{W},128). Thus, the embedding width remains 128, but the projection network’s capacity varies with the input dimension.

Sequence initialization.

The initial treatment input is the all-zero vector, used as a sequence-start placeholder rather than a treatment category. In particular, it differs from the CancerSim no-treatment category, encoded as (1,0,0,0)(1,0,0,0). Dataset-specific initialization of the outcome and raw current-state inputs is described in Appendix C. The first historical current-state slot is set directly to zero in the dcd_{c}-dimensional encoding space, before the WcW_{c} and WmW_{m} projections; it is not obtained by encoding a zero-valued raw input.

Temporal Network and Alignment Details

Let dhd_{h} denote the temporal hidden dimension. The learned multilayer-perceptron embeddings eXe_{X} and eYe_{Y} map the preceding treatment and outcome into ℝdh\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}, while the learned projection WcW_{c} maps the preceding current-state encoding into the same space. The history token at sequence position tt is

st=LNX⁡(eX​(Xt−1))+LNY⁡(eY​(Yt−1))+LNC⁡(Wc​ct−1),s_{t}=\operatorname{LN}_{X}(e_{X}(X_{t-1}))+\operatorname{LN}_{Y}(e_{Y}(Y_{t-1}))+\operatorname{LN}_{C}(W_{c}c_{t-1}), (13)

where LNX\operatorname{LN}_{X}, LNY\operatorname{LN}_{Y}, and LNC\operatorname{LN}_{C} are separately parameterized layer-normalization operators.

Let PE\operatorname{PE} denote the addition of fixed sinusoidal positional encodings to the token sequence. A second learned projection, WmW_{m}, maps the historical current-state encodings to the cross-attention memory. The temporal network produces

ht−1=[TD(PE(s1:T),Wmc0:T−1;M,Mpad)]t,h_{t-1}=\left[\operatorname{TD}\!\left(\operatorname{PE}(s_{1:T}),W_{m}c_{0:T-1};M,M_{\mathrm{pad}}\right)\right]_{t}, (14)

where TT is the padded sequence length, TD\operatorname{TD} is the stack of temporal Transformer decoder blocks, and [⋅]t[\cdot]_{t} selects its output at position tt. The first input supplies the position-encoded tokens, and the second supplies the historical memory without added positional encoding. These decoder blocks implement the historical encoder 𝒯\mathcal{T}; the direct treatment-plan decoder is a separate module.

Both attention paths use the causal mask MM, with Mt​j=0M_{tj}=0 for j≤tj\leq t and Mt​j=−∞M_{tj}=-\infty otherwise. Here tt indexes query positions and jj indexes key positions. The key-padding mask MpadM_{\mathrm{pad}} excludes inactive positions. Since position jj contains inputs aligned with time j−1j-1, the output at position tt depends only on observations available through time t−1t-1.

At the first sequence position, X0X_{0} is an all-zero start placeholder. The initial outcome input Y0Y_{0} is zero for CVSim and the standardized observed initial tumor volume for CancerSim. The initial historical encoding c0c_{0} is set directly to zero in the encoding space before applying WcW_{c} and WmW_{m}. The current encoding ctc_{t} remains outside this shifted stream and is fused with ht−1h_{t-1} after temporal processing.

HiSTOR Optimization Details

Auxiliary treatment prediction.

Let 𝒦\mathcal{K} index the treatment categories, and let

pi​tX=softmax⁡(ℓi​tX)p_{it}^{X}=\operatorname{softmax}(\ell_{it}^{X})

denote the auxiliary treatment-probability vector for patient ii at time tt. Its kk-th element, pi​t,kXp_{it,k}^{X}, is the predicted probability of treatment category kk. For each minibatch, let ℐb\mathcal{I}_{b} denote the valid patient–time observations. The auxiliary treatment loss is

ℒX=−1|ℐb|∑(i,t)∈ℐb∑k∈𝒦𝟏{Xi​t=k}logpi​t,kX,\mathcal{L}_{X}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{b}|}\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{I}_{b}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\mathbf{1}\{X_{it}=k\}\log p_{it,k}^{X}, (15)

Both simulation datasets encode each treatment choice as one categorical label; in CancerSim, the category representing both therapies is treated as a single treatment class. The auxiliary treatment loss is not weighted by treatment frequency, and its contribution to the backbone objective is scaled by λX\lambda_{X}.

The complete backbone objective is given in Equation 6, where ee is the training epoch and the λ\lambda coefficients weight the corresponding objectives.

Regularization and updates.

The backbone uses (λX,λroll)=(0.01,0.25)(\lambda_{X},\lambda_{\mathrm{roll}})=(0.01,0.25) for CVSim and (1,0)(1,0) for CancerSim. The latent-norm coefficient is λnorm=0.01\lambda_{\mathrm{norm}}=0.01.

The encoding critic DcD_{c} compares the current-state encoding ctc_{t} with standard-normal samples ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,Idc)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d_{c}}), where IdcI_{d_{c}} is the dcd_{c}-dimensional identity matrix. The embedding critic DuD_{u} compares generated embeddings GV​(ϵ)G_{V}(\epsilon) with observed embeddings utu_{t}. The encoder and generator minimize

ℒE,adv=−𝔼⁡[Dc​(ct)],ℒG,adv=−𝔼⁡[Du​(GV​(ϵ))].\mathcal{L}_{E,\mathrm{adv}}=-\mathbb{E}[D_{c}(c_{t})],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{G,\mathrm{adv}}=-\mathbb{E}[D_{u}(G_{V}(\epsilon))]. (16)

The adversarial term in Equation 6 is the sum of the encoder and generator objectives:

ℒadv=ℒE,adv+ℒG,adv.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}}=\mathcal{L}_{E,\mathrm{adv}}+\mathcal{L}_{G,\mathrm{adv}}. (17)

These distributional objectives act on the first-level encoding and embedding spaces. The critics use Wasserstein losses with gradient penalties (Gulrajani et al., 2017) and jointly minimize

ℒD=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{D}={} 𝔼ℐ​[Dc​(ct)]−𝔼ϵ​[Dc​(ϵ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{I}}[D_{c}(c_{t})]-\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}[D_{c}(\epsilon)] (18)
+𝔼ϵ​[Du​(GV​(ϵ))]−𝔼ℐ​[Du​(ut)]\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}[D_{u}(G_{V}(\epsilon))]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{I}}[D_{u}(u_{t})]
+λgp​(ℛgpc+ℛgpu).\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{gp}}\left(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{gp}}^{c}+\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{gp}}^{u}\right).

During critic updates, the current-state representations and generated samples are detached from the remaining network. For each critic, the gradient penalty is

ℛgp​(D)=𝔼v~​[(‖∇v~D​(v~)‖2−1)2],\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{gp}}(D)=\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{v}}\left[\left(\|\nabla_{\widetilde{v}}D(\widetilde{v})\|_{2}-1\right)^{2}\right], (19)

where

v~=α​vref+(1−α)​vmodel,α∼𝒰⁡(0,1).\widetilde{v}=\alpha v_{\mathrm{ref}}+(1-\alpha)v_{\mathrm{model}},\qquad\alpha\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1).

The paired reference and model inputs are (ϵ,ct)(\epsilon,c_{t}) for DcD_{c} and (ut,GV​(ϵ))(u_{t},G_{V}(\epsilon)) for DuD_{u}. We use λgp=10\lambda_{\mathrm{gp}}=10 and perform three critic updates for each backbone update.

The latent-norm penalty is

ℒnorm=𝔼ℐ​[(‖ct‖22dc−1)2],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{norm}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{I}}\left[\left(\frac{\|c_{t}\|_{2}^{2}}{d_{c}}-1\right)^{2}\right], (20)

with λnorm=0.01\lambda_{\mathrm{norm}}=0.01. This term regulates the normalized latent scale around one, while distribution matching is handled by the adversarial objective. With zero-based epoch index ee, the adversarial coefficient is

λadv​(e)=0.01​min⁡(1,max⁡(0,e−1020)).\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}(e)=0.01\min\!\left(1,\max\!\left(0,\frac{e-10}{20}\right)\right). (21)

The CVSim rollout coefficient remains 0.250.25 throughout training, without an additional warm-up schedule. The CVSim backbone rollout horizon is five steps. Training samples one origin uniformly from the complete valid five-step windows of each eligible trajectory. At rollout offset jj, the current- and previous-treatment input arrays are masked at positions later than t+jt+j, so later treatment entries are not exposed to earlier predictions. Generated outcomes remain connected to the computational graph when they are inserted into subsequent history inputs. Validation uses one deterministically selected middle valid origin for each eligible trajectory.

For CVSim, let ρk\rho_{k} denote the empirical proportion of treatment category kk in the training data. The treatment weight for category kk is computed once as

wk=ρk−1/2∑ℓ∈𝒦ρℓρℓ−1/2.w_{k}=\frac{\rho_{k}^{-1/2}}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{K}}\rho_{\ell}\rho_{\ell}^{-1/2}}. (22)

These weights are used for the backbone one-step outcome loss and for the direct decoder training and validation losses. They are not used for the auxiliary treatment loss, the backbone rollout loss, or the backbone validation criterion. CancerSim uses unit weights throughout.

Outcome and rollout losses.

Let wXi​tw_{X_{it}} be the weight of the observed treatment category. The factual one-step outcome loss is

ℒY=∑(i,t)∈ℐbwXi​t​‖y^i​t​(Xi​t)−Yi​t‖22dy​∑(i,t)∈ℐbwXi​t,\mathcal{L}_{Y}=\frac{\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{I}_{b}}w_{X_{it}}\left\|\widehat{y}_{it}(X_{it})-Y_{it}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{d_{y}\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{I}_{b}}w_{X_{it}}}, (23)

where dyd_{y} is the outcome dimension. CVSim uses the training-derived treatment weights defined above, whereas CancerSim uses unit weights.

For CVSim, let 𝒲b(5)\mathcal{W}_{b}^{(5)} be the sampled valid five-step factual windows in a minibatch. The rollout prediction y^i,t+jroll\widehat{y}^{\mathrm{roll}}_{i,t+j} is generated recursively, with each prediction supplied to the subsequent history. The rollout loss is

ℒroll=∑(i,t)∈𝒲b(5)∑j=04‖y^i,t+jroll−Yi,t+j‖225​dy​|𝒲b(5)|,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}}=\frac{\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{W}_{b}^{(5)}}\sum_{j=0}^{4}\left\|\widehat{y}^{\mathrm{roll}}_{i,t+j}-Y_{i,t+j}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{5d_{y}\,|\mathcal{W}_{b}^{(5)}|}, (24)

and does not use treatment weights. CancerSim sets λroll=0\lambda_{\mathrm{roll}}=0.

Direct-decoder architecture.

At the prediction origin, the decoder forms

βt=tanh⁡(Wb​[Zt,sistat,y~t−1]).\beta_{t}=\tanh\!\left(W_{b}[Z_{t},s_{i}^{\mathrm{stat}},\widetilde{y}_{t-1}]\right).

Here WbW_{b} is learned and y~t−1\widetilde{y}_{t-1} is the dataset-specific previous-outcome input. Here sistats_{i}^{\mathrm{stat}} denotes the static decoder input: patient-factor features in CVSim and the patient-type feature in CancerSim. The main-text expression Dτ​(Zt,x¯)D_{\tau}(Z_{t},\bar{x}) is a high-level shorthand; the implementation also supplies sistats_{i}^{\mathrm{stat}} and the prepared previous-outcome input y~t−1\widetilde{y}_{t-1} at the prediction boundary. A shared treatment-plan GRU and horizon-specific heads then produce

ηk=GRU⁡(EX​(xt+k),ηk−1),y^t+kD=gk​([βt,ηk]),η−1=βt,\eta_{k}=\operatorname{GRU}(E_{X}(x_{t+k}),\eta_{k-1}),\qquad\widehat{y}_{t+k}^{\mathrm{D}}=g_{k}([\beta_{t},\eta_{k}]),\quad\eta_{-1}=\beta_{t},

for k=0,…,τ−1k=0,\ldots,\tau-1. Here EXE_{X} is the decoder treatment embedding and gkg_{k} is the outcome head at offset kk. Generated outcomes are not fed between heads.

Direct-decoder objective.

After backbone selection, the exponential-moving-average backbone is frozen and used to extract decoder contexts without gradients. Let 𝒲\mathcal{W} be a minibatch of complete factual windows indexed by patient ii and prediction origin tt, let τ\tau be the number of target steps, and let dyd_{y} be the outcome dimension. The direct decoder minimizes

ℒdir=∑(i,t)∈𝒲∑j=0τ−1wXi,t+j​‖y^i,t+jD−Yi,t+j‖22dy​∑(i,t)∈𝒲∑j=0τ−1wXi,t+j.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dir}}=\frac{\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{W}}\sum_{j=0}^{\tau-1}w_{X_{i,t+j}}\|\widehat{y}^{\mathrm{D}}_{i,t+j}-Y_{i,t+j}\|_{2}^{2}}{d_{y}\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{W}}\sum_{j=0}^{\tau-1}w_{X_{i,t+j}}}. (25)

Here y^i,t+jD\widehat{y}^{\mathrm{D}}_{i,t+j} is the direct prediction at horizon offset jj, and wXi,t+jw_{X_{i,t+j}} is the weight assigned to the observed treatment category at that step. CVSim uses the training-derived treatment weights defined above, whereas CancerSim uses unit weights. Decoder checkpoints are selected using the corresponding factual validation objective.

Backbone training uses AdamW with separate learning-rate groups for the current-state autoencoder and the remaining non-critic modules, together with a separate optimizer for the critics. Gradients are clipped to norm 11. An exponential moving average with decay 0.990.99 is maintained for the backbone and is used for validation, one-step prediction, and decoder-context extraction. Decoder contexts are extracted without gradients after backbone selection.

The direct decoder uses AdamW with learning rate 10−310^{-3}, weight decay 10−310^{-3}, gradient clipping at norm 11, no parameter averaging, hidden width 3232, batch size 40964096, early-stopping patience 2020, and a maximum training budget of 200200 epochs. Decoder windows contain only valid targets and exclude the first sequence position, which lacks a genuine preceding outcome. The decoder uses all four latent branches of ZtZ_{t}; its treatment GRU shares parameters across horizons, while each horizon has an independent outcome head.

Appendix C Data and Evaluation Protocols

CVSim

CVSim is a stochastic longitudinal dynamical system in which a six-dimensional state evolves with the preceding categorical treatment and a three-dimensional observed patient-factor vector. Four noisy state projections form the base time-varying covariates. Treatment is sampled from a three-category softmax mechanism depending on the covariates and patient factor. The scalar outcome combines state and covariate contributions with treatment main effects and state-dependent treatment interactions. The observed configuration supplies the patient factor as static input.

For the current-state projection, CVSim directly uses the observed covariate vector. Under the implementation-only notation introduced in Appendix A,

Wi​t=Vi​t.W_{it}=V_{it}.

Thus, dW=7+dhdd_{W}=7+d_{\mathrm{hd}}, consisting of the four base time-varying covariates, the three observed patient factors supplied as static inputs, and any additional dimensions. The preceding-outcome channel is initialized to zero at the sequence start.

The additional dimensions are not pure-noise features or separate latent patient factors. Each dimension is generated as a noisy linear measurement of the same three-dimensional observed patient-factor vector. These measurements are added after the base trajectories have been generated and therefore do not directly alter the base treatment-assignment or outcome equations.

Writing qi∈ℝ3q_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} for the observed patient-factor vector and Whd∈ℝdhd×3W_{\mathrm{hd}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{hd}}\times 3} for a projection matrix sampled once for each simulated dataset, the extensions are

Vihd=Whd​qi+ϵi(Static),Vi,thd=Whd​qi+tT−1​𝟏dhd+ϵi,t(Temporal).V_{i}^{\mathrm{hd}}=W_{\mathrm{hd}}q_{i}+\epsilon_{i}\quad\text{(Static)},\qquad V_{i,t}^{\mathrm{hd}}=W_{\mathrm{hd}}q_{i}+\frac{t}{T-1}\mathbf{1}_{d_{\mathrm{hd}}}+\epsilon_{i,t}\quad\text{(Temporal)}.

The entries of WhdW_{\mathrm{hd}} are drawn independently from 𝒩⁡(0,0.52)\mathcal{N}(0,0.5^{2}), and the entries of the measurement-noise vectors are drawn independently from 𝒩⁡(0,0.32)\mathcal{N}(0,0.3^{2}). Thus, conditional on qiq_{i}, the noise components are independent, but the complete added measurements are not generally independent because they share the signal Whd​qiW_{\mathrm{hd}}q_{i}. In the Static setting, ϵi\epsilon_{i} is sampled once per patient and the resulting measurements are held fixed over time. In the Temporal setting, ϵi,t\epsilon_{i,t} is resampled independently for each time point, and a common linear drift is added.

Consequently, increasing dhdd_{\mathrm{hd}} increases the number of noisy, redundant observed measurements rather than the number of underlying patient factors; the patient-factor dimension remains three. The two extension modes coincide when dhd=0d_{\mathrm{hd}}=0. The simulator generates potential outcomes for all three treatments at every time point. For multi-step evaluation, it starts from the factual state at the forecast origin and reuses the exogenous noise under the fixed treatment plan. The resulting future covariates are not supplied to the prediction models.

CancerSim

CancerSim simulates tumor volume Yi​tY_{it} using Gompertz-type growth, chemotherapy concentration, linear and quadratic radiotherapy effects, and multiplicative noise. The simulator has no separate time-varying covariate channel beyond the tumor-volume trajectory. The patient-type feature SiS_{i} is a baseline covariate that modifies the treatment-response coefficients. Accordingly, the CancerSim covariate variable in the general formulation contains the baseline component SiS_{i}, while tumor volume remains the outcome Yi​tY_{it}.

Treatment probabilities at time tt depend on the recent mean tumor diameter computed from the observed outcome history Yi,<tY_{i,<t}. Past outcomes therefore belong to the observed pre-treatment history and provide time-varying confounding information, while retaining their definition as outcomes.

For the implemented current-state projection, the raw input is constructed as

Wi​t=[Yi,t−1,Si].W_{it}=[Y_{i,t-1},S_{i}].

Here Wi​tW_{it} is an implementation-only input tensor; this construction does not redefine the outcome Yi,t−1Y_{i,t-1} as a covariate. The first input uses the observed initial tumor volume after dataset-level standardization, and the static patient-type feature is repeated across time. Hence dW=2d_{W}=2, and the projection expands this two-dimensional input to the 16-dimensional current-state encoding ctc_{t}. The initial historical outcome input is the standardized baseline tumor volume.

The training, validation, one-step counterfactual, and multi-step counterfactual cohorts are generated separately. Counterfactual expansion produces multiple evaluation entries per patient; these entries must not be counted as independent patients. The one-step test includes factual prefixes and alternative-treatment branches, and its metric scores all active entries rather than only the final counterfactual position of each branch.

Initial diameters follow a truncated log-normal stage mixture. For stages I, II, IIIA, IIIB, and IV, the log-scale (μ,σ)(\mu,\sigma) pairs are (1.72,4.70)(1.72,4.70), (1.96,1.63)(1.96,1.63), (1.91,9.40)(1.91,9.40), (2.76,6.87)(2.76,6.87), and (3.86,8.82)(3.86,8.82), with sampling weights 1432, 128, 1306, 7248, and 12840. The lower diameter bound is 0.3; the upper bound is 5 for stage I and 13 otherwise. Diameters are converted to volumes. Factual trajectories stop at the death threshold, stochastic recovery, or the maximum length. Outcome and patient-type scaling statistics are fitted on training data; treatment indicators retain their categorical encoding.

Appendix D Forecast Boundary and Model Adaptations

For fixed-regime multi-step evaluation in CVSim, Ys−1Y_{s-1} and VsV_{s} remain observed, later previous-outcome slots are cleared, and future covariate placeholders repeat VsV_{s}. Models may mask, replace, or bypass these placeholders. In CancerSim, the boundary outcome is first predicted under the factual boundary treatment and inserted into the subsequent history. This bridge is not scored; the five fixed-plan targets correspond to horizons two through six. Scoring uses each model’s multi-step output directly, without replacing its first scored entry with a separate one-step prediction.

Appendix E Metric Definitions and Aggregation

We report normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE); lower values are better. The normalization constants are defined without using model predictions: CancerSim uses the simulator’s fixed tumor-death volume threshold, whereas CVSim uses ranges computed from the corresponding test targets. For CancerSim one-step prediction, let mi​tm_{it} mark an active expanded test entry and let 𝒯+={t:∑imi​t>0}\mathcal{T}_{+}=\{t:\sum_{i}m_{it}>0\}. The reported error is

EC,1=100DC​1|𝒯+|​∑t∈𝒯+∑imi​t​(y^i​t−yi​t)2∑imi​t.E_{C,1}=\frac{100}{D_{C}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{+}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{+}}\frac{\sum_{i}m_{it}(\widehat{y}_{it}-y_{it})^{2}}{\sum_{i}m_{it}}}. (26)

Here ii indexes counterfactually expanded test entries and DC=π​133/6≈1150.3465D_{C}=\pi 13^{3}/6\approx 1150.3465 is the simulator’s tumor-death threshold. Thus CancerSim first averages squared error across active entries at each time and then averages across valid times; it does not pool all active entries before taking the square root.

For CVSim one-step prediction, let ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} contain all active patient–time–treatment entries. With DV,1D_{V,1} equal to the range of their target potential outcomes,

EV,1=100max⁡(DV,1,10−8)​1|ℐ1|​∑(i,t,a)∈ℐ1(y^i​t​(a)−yi​t​(a))2.E_{V,1}=\frac{100}{\max(D_{V,1},10^{-8})}\sqrt{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{1}|}\sum_{(i,t,a)\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}(\widehat{y}_{it}(a)-y_{it}(a))^{2}}. (27)

This definition pools the active test units, time points, and all three current treatment arms.

For scored multi-step position hh, let ℐh\mathcal{I}_{h} contain the entries with finite predictions and targets. The horizon-specific error is

Eh=100max⁡(D,10−8)​1|ℐh|​∑i∈ℐh(y^i,h−yi,h)2.E_{h}=\frac{100}{\max(D,10^{-8})}\sqrt{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{h}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{h}}(\widehat{y}_{i,h}-y_{i,h})^{2}}. (28)

CancerSim uses D=DCD=D_{C} and reports horizons 22 through 66 after the unscored bridge prediction. CVSim uses the range of all fixed-regime multi-step targets across patients and the five scored positions, shared across horizons within the same seed and condition, and reports horizons 11 through 55. This rollout denominator differs from DV,1D_{V,1} because the one-step and multi-step evaluations use different target arrays. With the same simulator seed and patient split, adding high-dimensional measurements leaves the outcome trajectories unchanged, so the CVSim rollout denominator is constant across dimensions within a seed but may differ across seeds.

Within seed rr, the horizon average is E¯(r)=15​∑h=15Eh(r)\overline{E}^{(r)}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{h=1}^{5}E_{h}^{(r)}. For either a one-step score, a horizon-specific score, or this average, we report the mean and sample standard deviation across seeds {3,101,42,8,9}\{3,101,42,8,9\}, using denominator R−1R-1 with R=5R=5. No errors are pooled across datasets.

Appendix F Baselines and Training Configurations

The comparison uses HiSTOR and the seven baselines listed in Section 5.1. All methods receive the same simulated data realization, split, intervention regime, forecast boundary, and seed within each experimental condition. CancerSim uses 10,000 training and 1,000 validation patients, together with separate 1,000-patient one-step and multi-step test cohorts. CVSim uses an 80/10/10 patient split of 5,000 trajectories. Counterfactual test targets are used only for evaluation.

CRN uses an encoder LSTM with hidden width 24, balancing width 12, and head width 36, followed by a one-layer decoder with balancing width 18 and head width 36. Its encoder and decoder use Adam with learning rates 10−210^{-2} and 10−310^{-3} and batch sizes 128 and 1,024, respectively. CT uses one Transformer layer, two heads, dropout 0.1, and EMA decay 0.99; its CancerSim sequence/balancing/head widths vary across dataset-specific configurations, while CVSim uses widths 16/12/24. RMSN retains its four propensity, history, encoder, and decoder stages with dataset-specific widths, learning rates, batch sizes, and clipping thresholds.

Causal CPC uses dataset-specific local, context, and head widths with six-step contrastive prediction and an autoregressive treatment-plan decoder; its representation and outcome modules use AdamW and its treatment adversary uses SGD. CTD-NKO uses condition-specific CancerSim widths and a 24-dimensional CVSim model, with Adam, EMA, and validation-based selection. IGC-Net uses a 16/8/4 CancerSim hidden/history/head configuration and a 48/88/44 CVSim configuration; multi-step prediction fits a separate fixed-regime model for each required treatment-plan prefix. MSM uses unregularized multinomial logistic propensity models, stabilized weights clipped at the first and 99th percentiles, and weighted linear outcome regressions.

HiSTOR uses a 16-dimensional current-covariate encoding, a 128-dimensional four-layer, four-head Transformer with feed-forward width 256, and a 160-dimensional structured representation split into widths 24/24/48/64. The backbone uses AdamW with learning rates 10−310^{-3} for the main generator, 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} for the autoencoder modules, and 10−410^{-4} for the critics, together with gradient-penalty weight 10, three critic updates, and EMA decay 0.99. The direct treatment-plan decoder has hidden width 32, uses all four representation branches, and is trained with AdamW at learning rate 10−310^{-3}, weight decay 10−310^{-3}, batch size 4,096, and gradient clipping at 1. The selected backbone remains frozen during decoder training.

CRN, CT, and RMSN use fixed training budgets, while HiSTOR, Causal CPC, CTD-NKO, and IGC-Net use the validation and checkpoint-selection criteria reported in Table 9. All stochastic experiments use the five reported evaluation seeds.

G.1 Paired Comparisons

We compare HiSTOR with the strongest external baseline identified by the cross-seed mean in each condition. HiSTOR achieves a lower mean within-seed NRMSE difference in every CancerSim condition. It wins in three or more of the five seeds for every independent one-step comparison and in all five seeds for every five-horizon-average comparison. The tables report the mean paired difference, defined as HiSTOR minus the comparator, together with approximate 95% t intervals across the five seeds.

Appendix I MIMIC-III Semi-Synthetic Evaluation

Data and protocol.

To complement the controlled simulation studies, we evaluate HiSTOR on MIMIC-III ICU covariates processed using the MIMIC-Extract pipeline (Johnson et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020), followed by the IGC-Net semi-synthetic outcome and treatment generator (Hess et al., 2026). This is a semi-synthetic counterfactual benchmark, not a real-outcome clinical prediction experiment. The cohort contains 1,000 patients with a patient-level split of 600/200/200 for training, validation, and testing. Each raw trajectory contains 30–50 time points; the upstream indexing shift makes the effective model sequence one time point shorter. The benchmark has three binary treatment variables and two synthetic outcomes. We use seeds {3,101,42,8,9}\{3,101,42,8,9\}. At τ=1\tau=1, we evaluate one-step counterfactual prediction. For τ=2,…,6\tau=2,\ldots,6, we evaluate multi-step prediction under the six-step treatment plan [0,0,1][0,0,1] repeated at every step.

Comparison protocol.

We include CT (Melnychuk et al., 2022) and IGC-Net (Hess et al., 2026) as two strong prior methods with released support for this benchmark. CT and IGC-Net use their released official implementations and configurations, whereas HiSTOR uses its model-specific configuration. All three models share the same cached cohort, patient split, seeds, forecast boundary, and evaluation implementation. The table reports arithmetic means over the five seeds.

CT achieves the lowest one-step error at τ=1\tau=1, whereas HiSTOR achieves the lowest error among the three evaluated methods at every multi-step horizon τ=2,…,6\tau=2,\ldots,6. Relative to CT, the strongest competing method at these horizons, HiSTOR reduces error by approximately 0.3%0.3\%, 4.4%4.4\%, 0.2%0.2\%, 5.8%5.8\%, and 6.5%6.5\%, respectively. These results provide complementary evidence for HiSTOR’s multi-step prediction performance on clinically grounded covariates under the semi-synthetic fixed-treatment protocol.
